t: The Three Best Arguments Against a Knowledge Rich Curriculum
q: In the age of social media, it’s easy to enter a debate in bad faith, defaulting to your ‘tribe’ and presuming bad intentions of those who disagree with you. I think that this is not only a pretty depressing worldview, it’s just straightforwardly incorrect.
You can’t directly teach skills; they arise from, and supervene upon, knowledge. And not all knowledge is equal.

Experts who think critically, in the way that we want children to, are in fact doing a huge amount of work under the surface. They effortlessly and unconsciously select, assimilate and compare thousands of facts stored in their long-term memory.

Biologically secondary knowledge is effortful and difficult and our brains are not really designed through evolution to engage in thinking in this way. As a result, even with a good enquiry question, we will often opt out of thinking about the hardest stuff, allow others to carry the cognitive load, or simply be unaware of what it is we are supposed to be learning.

Essentially, the enquiry model in most cases is what I call the ‘fingers crossed’ approach. Maybe they will stumble across lots of knowledge, and understand it, and construct amazing ideas that stick for life. But maybe they won’t.

It is not necessary to write a powerpoint on the Romans, or a story about the Battle of Hastings, or a diagram of the water cycle, or multiple examples of direct speech being punctuated correctly (or incorrectly) to exercise autonomy in delivering these lessons.

t: What If You're Happier at Work?
q: What I learned on maternity leave, was not only how much I loved being a mother, but how much I had been seriously misjudging how hard it was to be a stay-at-home parent for my entire life.

Being a mom does not mean prevent me from having other goals, dreams, and ambitions that belong to just me. My job provides me with a sense of purpose and fulfillment that I am a happier person for having, and that helps me show up more purposefully and intentionally as a parent.
The answer is neither. It’s better to do what you want. I recognize that sounds flippant but in actuality it is factual.

Most of the compelling findings do not suggest there is some simple working-versus-stay-at-home binary answer but instead, that the importance of the fit between a mother’s preferences, her actual circumstances, the quality of caregiving she provides, and the support available to her trump any individual working arrangement.
What the science has shown has consistent negative effects, is when parents are forced into a working or caregiving arrangement that does not match their goals or desires.
If you want to work, you should not feel guilty for finding fulfillment in a career. If you prefer to stay home and raise your children instead, you should not need to justify that choice.

What stood out most to me was how often regret was tied not to the arrangement, but to feeling forced into it. The lack of choice, rather than the choice itself, seemed to weigh most heavily on parents.

t: The AP quandary and how to resolve it
a: Chester E. Finn, Jr. and Michael J. Petrilli
q: The Advanced Placement program is its biggest revenue generator and, along with the SAT, its showpiece. But where the SAT is little more than a measuring-and-comparison tool, the AP operation has long served as an indicator of educational quality and performance, often seen as the “gold standard” of high school achievement.

Should the Board make it harder to pass a college-level course than the colleges do? Bear in mind that 19 of its 31 trustees have day jobs in higher ed, often engaged in “enrollment management” for individual institutions.
But it’s also well known that poor and minority students are far likelier to enroll in AP courses than to pass AP exams.

So yes, the College Board has done some succumbing, most obviously by changing how student work on some of its most popular exams is evaluated, thereby boosting the shares of test-takers who pass and those who get high scores.

But is it realistic to expect a nonprofit organization—one that depends for its existence on clients and institutions that find it useful—to continue to resist changes in the zeitgeist that surrounds it?

We agree with some of the AP program’s critics that it’s a shame—and a problem for the country—that these widely respected tests appear to have gotten easier over time. As discussed above, we understand why that’s happened. And we understand that it’s hard to reverse, especially because it’s unclear what “standard” the AP should peg itself to, if not “a level of performance equivalent to passing an introductory college course.

First, in the interest of transparency, the College Board could declare that scores of 2 ought now to count as “passing” given the decline in college standards, making clear that this isn’t the Board’s preference but its acceptance of current reality, however regrettable.

In other words, the College Board should use the AP scoring system to differentiate the performance of students more clearly than today by acknowledging that a 2 indicates readiness to pass courses in most colleges in this time of grade inflation, while saving 5s for students at the very top of the performance distribution, making the Advanced Placement program at least 22-karat-gold-worthy again.

q: The attention-learning link goes well beyond keeping students from fooling around on devices in class (although that’s also an important issue, and one that we’ll come back to in a second). There’s a deeper connection to a core principle about memory, which is that we form nearly no memories in the absence of attention.

There’s no such backup tape buried in the brain, of course; the reality is that we retain only a miniscule amount of what we experience, and generally only those experiences that are juiced by a generous dose of attention.
Our position was that digital distraction affected people all across the age spectrum, and we also believed that students themselves could come up with creative solutions to the problem.
Lastly, we didn’t stop at prescribing what students should and shouldn’t do in regard to managing distractions – we ended with a module on how to make good intentions stick over time.
Essentially, present-you sets up constraints that make it easier for future-you to do the right thing, regardless of how tired, tempted, or rebellious future-you happens to be feeling.

t: Overcoming Impostor Syndrome
q: Impostor Syndrome is the personal conviction that one’s professional success is undeserved, and that sooner or later others will notice and expose the deception.
Across four studies of 3,600 people, MIT’s Basima Tewfik found that team members with more frequent impostor thoughts performed just as well and were seen as more interpersonally effective.
Doubt about themselves actually made them more other-focused. They asked more questions and listened more intently. The problem is rarely the thought itself.
It is what people do to manage those thoughts, such as over-preparing, procrastinating, discounting praise, and taking less risk, that creates real issues.

Because the impostor cycle survives by crediting every success to luck or last-minute heroics, the remedy is to audit the credit . After each win, a leader should write down the specific decisions they made that shaped the outcome.

Impostor feelings thrive on isolation. Because each person sees everyone else’s polished surface and compares it to their own messy interior, group conversations where peers get the chance to discover that their doubts are shared can work wonders.
A leader who says plainly, “I felt like a fraud my first year on this job,” gives everyone else permission to stop pretending.

A leader may never silence the voice that says they are a fraud, but they can stop letting it run their life. Feeling like you don’t belong in the role is often the surest sign you’re growing into it.

t: Maggie's Library
q: What changed things for Maggie wasn’t a reading scheme. It was a badly dubbed TV serialisation of Heidi. She loved the story so much that she found the book, probably at her local library, and read it for herself.

The story came before the skill. That’s exactly what we heard at the Open University’s Reading for Pleasure conference: a love of reading doesn’t come from doing everything “right”. It grows through connection.

A child who found reading hard was read as a child who couldn’t, or wouldn’t, learn. At school, she says, she used to pretend to fall asleep because she just wasn’t engaged. Every time we lower our expectations of a child because of where they come from, or how they arrived at our door, we risk writing their story for them.
Her father, who had dreamed of studying medicine, took her to Foyles bookshop on Charing Cross Road. To Maggie, it was “almost like a pilgrimage”.

At her 13th school, her records had been “scattered to the four winds”, and she was asked which stream she was usually in. She had always been in the bottom stream. This time, she told them she should be in the top one. They believed her, and she worked to prove them right.
You do need someone to believe in you,” Maggie said. For her, that was her father. “It might take you longer,” he told her, “but it doesn’t mean you can’t get there.
Whenever Maggie’s father bought a book, he wrote in the front in green ink. When she was 14 or 15, he gave her The Wind in the Willows, and inside it he wrote “Maggie’s library”.
But I keep thinking about Maggie at the Puffin Book Club, being told she shouldn’t get a book this time. For some children, a book of their own is never a given.

t: Lessons from the First Great Enrollment Decline
q: How well do institutional leaders learn from the lessons of the past? If school districts are the institutions in question, the answer is: not well at all.

Between fall 2019 and fall 2024, enrollment in public elementary and secondary schools fell nationally by 1.4 million students (2.8 percent). Forty states have experienced declines, and enrollment is projected to keep dropping—by an additional 2.7 million students by 2031 and even further by 2050.

Why do districts often avoid or delay responding to declining enrollments? Because managing contraction is much more difficult than managing growth. District leaders must confront political conflict, deep-seated professional norms, and internal bureaucratic resistance.
In Austin, Texas, the district has lost 20 percent of its enrollment, more than 17,000 students, over the last 15 years and now faces a deficit amounting to 20 percent of its budget.

During periods of growth, districts add new programs, hire additional staff and administrators, and create new layers of organizational authority. These increments become embedded in the system, making it difficult to cut them later.
Muddling through may postpone conflict, but it can also result in a slow and painful death from malnutrition.

Declining enrollment creates a zero-sum dynamic with no slack resources and clear winners and losers. This dramatically intensifies conflict among stakeholders. Growth can mask errors in judgment, but the management of decline requires leaders who can identify challenges before they become crises and diffuse conflict among competing interests.
Education leaders must have the courage to acknowledge that the traditional model was not designed for retrenchment and must be reinvented for flexibility and adaptation.

t: Learning to Choose: Being Present Together
a: Jennifer W. Shewmaker and Julie Crum
q: Presence asks us to listen long enough to understand an idea and to ask questions when we are confused. It also asks us to stay engaged when the conversation becomes difficult.

For the students in my assessment class, I decided that they needed the opportunity to connect what they were learning in the course with the work they hoped to do in the future. In other words, they needed to understand the why behind learning this material.
What we’ve found is that the key is to be intentional in naming presence, why it matters, and explicitly providing the opportunity to practice it.

Instead of telling students to “Pay attention,” we can explain what that looks like. Young students might take a walk through the school, on the playground, or visit the school garden with the instructions to be super spies who are looking for details.

Oftentimes, teachers and school leaders can become overly focused on hitting academic benchmarks and goals to the point where we let distinctly human skills, such as the practice of presence, slide as we strive for better test scores. We are not programming machines, however.

Students who see presence modeled and are given the chance to practice it are more likely to practice it on their own. Children begin recognizing that belonging isn’t simply something we receive from a community. It’s also something we help create through our choices.

q: Over time, I’ve started thinking of kids like Handstand Girl and Smaller Boy as ‘Submarine Children’. That is, kids who can appear typically developing to a casual onlooker, but turn out not to be.

t: Get rich quick schema
q: A schema is a mental framework or map of connected ideas. These connections allow us to quickly leap between related concepts and problem solve based on ideas that our previous experiences tell us could apply to the situation.

If you have ever observed a truly expert teacher it may seem like they have a sixth sense, almost as if they are seeing the future before it happens and making adjustments to ensure that the ideal outcome happens.

In recently reading ‘Becoming an Expert Teacher’ by Nidhi Sachdeva and Paul Kirschner however I had an alarming thought. What if schemas are not always positive? I started spiralling a little bit thinking of the online educational discourse and the way our algorithms are set up to create an echo chamber for us which satisfies our confirmation bias.

A teacher may develop a schema that if a class is disruptive that yelling at and exiting a student leads the rest of the class to be calm. In that teacher’s mind there is now an A to B logic that if I shout and send them out then teaching will be more effective. Every time that scenario plays out it creates a stronger schema and therefore heuristic for the teacher to follow which may mean that they may never develop the expertise to best help the students in front of them.

On average teachers improve regardless of other factors for the first five years of their career and then plateau for the next two decades before having a slight decline. This tells me that unless schemas are continued to be challenged and built on after those first five years then teachers are likely to ‘do what works’ but what works isn’t necessarily what is best.

Don’t get me wrong, we definitely want students to be memorising key facts, however those facts are useless unless they know what the ideas and words within those facts mean. A student may memorise the definition that ‘inertia’ means an object resisting change in its state of motion but within that if the student doesn’t understand the word ‘resisting’ or ‘state of motion’ then they’ll be unable to apply their knowledge in new and novel contexts.

t: Our Present Affects Their Future

Our generation, just as all past generations have, make decisions in the present that have consequences borne primarily by future generations.
